title: Education Extra: Irish Education, Sunk Cost Fallacy and Wile E. Coyote Girdham, Julian
author: Girdham, Julian
summary: Irish post-primary teacher Julian Girdham uses the sunk cost fallacy as a lens to diagnose a defining feature of Ireland's education system: the tendency to continue investing in approaches that are demonstrably not working because the system has already invested so heavily in them that abandonment feels unthinkable. The Wile E. Coyote metaphor -- running off a cliff and continuing to run in mid-air until you look down -- describes how Ireland's education policymakers have continued to implement reform cycles without acknowledging they're suspended above a chasm. Girdham applies this analysis to specific features of the Irish system: junior cycle reform implementation and the persistent investment in assessment-driven pedagogy that evidence shows narrows the curriculum. The article is a personal reflection from a practitioner who has watched successive reform waves arrive and recede without addressing the underlying structural problems.
points: The sunk cost fallacy in education operates at an institutional level: systems that have trained an entire generation of teachers in a particular approach and based assessment regimes on it are structurally incapable of abandoning it even when evidence of failure accumulates.

Ireland's junior cycle reform exemplifies the Wile E. Coyote dynamic: the system insisted progress was happening long after teachers and students concluded that the central promise -- reducing exam pressure and broadening learning -- was not being delivered.

Assessment-driven pedagogy creates a particular form of institutional capture: once high-stakes assessment defines what counts as learning, every reform that doesn't change the assessment regime is absorbed and neutralized by teaching to the test.

Girdham's practitioner perspective highlights the emotional dimension of sunk cost: teachers who invested years adapting to a reform have a personal stake in its success that makes honest evaluation of failure psychologically costly.

Education reform cycles are not primarily technical failures but institutional failures to build self-correcting mechanisms -- honest evaluation, willingness to abandon sunk costs -- that would allow learning from experience.
